title: The U.S. Just Took Japan's K-pop Crown — And the $120M Quarter Is the Warning Shot
excerpt: K-pop album exports hit $120M in Q1 2026, and the U.S. passed Japan. The shift could change how agencies plan the next export push.
author: MEARROW Editorial Desk
content:
`K-pop album exports` hit `US$120 million` in the first quarter of 2026, but the raw total is only half the story. The more disruptive line in Korea Customs data published on April 28 is that the `United States`, not Japan, finished as the biggest overseas market for Korean albums. That reversal lands harder than another record-high graphic because it suggests the geography of physical fandom is being rewritten in real time. For years, Japan was the dependable center of gravity whenever agencies talked about where packaged music still moved at scale. Now the quarter has ended with America on top, and the industry has to decide whether that was a spike, a BTS-assisted distortion, or the first clean sign that the old export order has stopped describing reality. [Related: Why K-pop's Global Growth No Longer Guarantees Korean Demand](/en/news/kpop-korean-market-optional-global-paradox)

## The Quarter That Flipped The Old Order

### The record itself is not in dispute

Yonhap, AJU Press and Korea JoongAng Daily all matched on the core facts released by the Korea Customs Service on April 28. South Korea exported `US$120 million` worth of K-pop albums from January through March, up `159 percent` from a year earlier. That made `Q1 2026` the first quarter ever to clear the `US$100 million` threshold for album exports. The number is large enough on its own, but the pace matters just as much. Customs data said quarterly records have now been falling one after another since the third quarter of 2025, which means this is no longer a one-off jump that can be dismissed as a lucky release calendar.

### The real shock is who finished first

The country ranking is what gives the story its edge. Yonhap reported that the United States accounted for about `28 percent` of first-quarter exports, overtaking Japan, which had held the top spot until last year. AJU Press put the destination totals more concretely at `US$36 million` for the U.S. and `US$31 million` for Japan, with the European Union at `US$21 million`, China at `US$18 million` and Taiwan at `US$9 million`. That matters because Japan has long been treated as K-pop's safest physical-album market outside Korea itself: deep retail culture, established touring economics, and fan behavior already trained to reward collectible formats. If America is now outbuying Japan on albums, agencies are no longer looking at a niche Western vanity market. They are looking at a physical-demand center with strategic weight.

## Why Physical Albums Are Still Winning

### Fans are no longer buying only music

One reason this number looks strange to casual observers is that it seems to contradict the broader streaming era. Why would album exports keep exploding when listeners can access the songs instantly on their phones? The answer has been visible for a while inside the business. In its January 9 analysis, *The Korea Times* argued that K-pop albums are increasingly functioning less like simple music carriers and more like access products: merchandise, collectibles, identity markers and entry points into fan participation. Photocards, multi-version packaging, fansign lotteries and special-edition goods have changed what an "album" means in practice. The physical object is not competing with Spotify on convenience. It is competing on ownership, scarcity and fandom proof.

### The customs explanation fits that shift

The Korea Customs Service itself pointed to two forces behind the Q1 surge: the continued global expansion of K-pop fandoms and growing demand for physical albums amid fatigue with algorithm-driven streaming. That second point is easy to underestimate. In many music markets, passive listening has become frictionless and endless, but frictionless does not always mean emotionally satisfying. Physical albums create a sense of possession that streaming cannot, especially in fandoms where collecting is part of participation. Once that logic clicks, a purchase is no longer just about hearing the tracks. It becomes a way to support a bias, qualify for an event, complete a set, or own a piece of an era before it disappears.

![K-pop album exports chart showing the U.S. overtaking Japan in Q1 2026](/images/news/kpop-exports-us-overtakes-japan-1.webp)
_The ranking shift matters because it hints at where physical fandom is now monetizing most aggressively, not just where songs are being streamed._

## The Boom Comes With A Catch

### Overseas strength is covering a softer home market

That is where the April 28 headline becomes more complicated than a victory lap. Back on January 16, *The Korea Times* reported, also citing customs data, that annual K-pop album exports reached a record `US$301.7 million` in 2025. Yet the same report said overall album sales, including both domestic and overseas markets, fell for a second consecutive year to roughly `93.5 million` units, down from around `120 million` in 2023. In other words, exports are roaring ahead while the broader volume story inside the market looks less invincible than it did during peak bulk-buy years. The international business is getting bigger, but it is also getting more selective about which acts and which markets can carry that growth.

### The U.S. lead does not mean the structure is suddenly safe

There is another reason to resist easy triumphalism. A market can become larger and more fragile at the same time. If more export value is being driven by a smaller set of blockbuster acts, then the headline number may hide rising dependence on a few artists, a few fandoms and a few release windows that can still overpower the market by themselves. That is especially relevant in a year when BTS is active again and top-tier touring is pulling global attention back toward the very biggest names. A single quarter can tell you where the energy is. It cannot guarantee that the new hierarchy is evenly distributed across the rest of the field.

## MEARROW's View On The New Export Map

### America beating Japan once is not the deepest story

MEARROW reads this less as a one-quarter upset and more as a planning signal. If the U.S. is now the biggest market for Korean album exports, the implications run beyond a country ranking. Release timing, version design, retailer partnerships, logistics, marketing spend and even city-level tour strategy start to look different when agencies believe North American physical demand is not a side effect of global fandom but one of its core engines. The old model treated America as the place that mattered most for streaming prestige and brand optics while Japan mattered most for reliable packaged revenue. The new quarter suggests those categories are starting to bleed into each other.

### That creates pressure on every mid-tier label

The biggest companies can respond by scaling distribution and using established fandom machines to turn momentum into repeat business. Smaller labels face a harsher puzzle. They can see the same headline, but they do not automatically inherit the infrastructure that made the number possible. The more album demand shifts toward distant high-value markets, the more success depends on fulfillment, merchandise design, language localization and tour-linked conversion strategies that many agencies still do not execute at elite level. So yes, the April 28 customs data is bullish. It is also a warning that the next stage of K-pop globalization may reward operational depth as much as artist popularity.

## The Next Quarter Will Matter More Than The Headline

### One record is loud. A pattern is louder.

The easiest version of this story is that K-pop had a monster quarter and America beat Japan. The more useful version is that the market may be entering a new phase in which physical fandom keeps growing overseas even as the business inside Korea becomes harder to read through old volume metrics alone. If that pattern holds into the second and third quarters of 2026, agencies will have to stop talking about the U.S. as merely a prestige battlefield and start treating it as one of the central revenue arenas in the genre. That is the real reason this quarter matters. `K-pop album exports` did not just hit another record on April 28, 2026. They may have revealed that the industry's old map is already out of date.
